questions.question: Explain why labour law exists, the constitutional rights of both sides, and the LRA's three principles.
questions.expected_answer: An individual worker negotiates from weakness — the firm can wait, and one applicant among hundreds has no bargaining power — and industrial history showed where the unregulated bargain leads. The Constitution guarantees fair labour practices, the rights to form and join unions, to organise and bargain collectively, and to strike; employers hold mirror rights to organise and lock out. The LRA's principles: self-government (the parties regulate their own relationship through negotiated agreements — the state sets the framework, not the wage); majoritarianism (the majority union speaks for the workforce with organisational rights); consultation (employers must consult and disclose before decisions affecting workers, retrenchment above all).

questions.question: Match the three Acts to their jobs with provisions, and distinguish the collective bargaining institutions by level.
questions.expected_answer: LRA — rules of engagement: union rights, bargaining institutions, protected strikes and lock-outs, unfair dismissal protection, and the CCMA/Labour Court machinery. BCEA — the floor under every job: maximum hours and overtime rules, minimum leave (annual, sick, family, maternity), notice periods, bans on child and forced labour — minimums contracts may better but never undercut. COIDA — the safety net: employer-funded compensation for occupational injuries and diseases without lawsuits. Institutions: unions organise and negotiate; employers' organisations mirror them; bargaining councils host sector-level negotiation whose agreements can extend to the whole sector; workplace forums consult (not wage-bargain) inside a single large workplace.

questions.question: Distinguish conciliation, mediation and arbitration; place the courts; and explain the protected strike.
questions.expected_answer: At the CCMA — free and first for most disputes — conciliation has a commissioner facilitate the parties' OWN settlement (nothing imposed); mediation has the intermediary actively propose solutions the parties may accept or refuse; arbitration has the commissioner hear evidence and DECIDE, issuing a binding award. The ladder settles most disputes low because self-built settlements are kept willingly. Above stand the Labour Court (reviewing awards, interpreting statutes, ruling on strikes and retrenchments) and the Labour Appeal Court. A protected strike follows procedure — dispute referred, notice given — and shields strikers from dismissal for striking; an unprotected strike carries no shield.
